column13:
Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (solar) 
The City of Waltham’s zoning code effectively limited large-scale solar energy facilities to industrial zones. A developer who owned land in Waltham and a neighboring town sought permission from the city building inspector to build an access road on the land the developer owned in Waltham to a proposed 1-MW solar facility in a neighboring town. The building inspector denied permission on the basis of local zoning restrictions. On June 4, 2022, the Supreme Judicial Court struck down the restrictions, finding that “[a]n outright ban of large-scale solar energy systems in all but one to two percent of a municipality’s land area . . . restricts rather than promotes the legislative goal of promoting solar energy” and that, “in the absence of a reasonable basis grounded in public health, safety, or welfare, such a prohibition is impermissible.”  Note that this is included as a pre-March 2022 development because the relevant restriction was in place before March 2022.

The revised bylaw would have banned energy storage systems as a principal use in all zoning districts and limited large-scale solar installations (defined as installations between 1.5 and 15 acres of land) to a special use in Forest Conservation Districts, prohibiting such installations in all other districts. The Massachusetts Attorney General’s office sent a letter to Shutesbury officials disapproving of the January 2023 bylaw, partially based on a determination that the bylaw violated state law by effectively banning solar installations. The Attorney General’s office’s action resulted in the pre-2023 bylaw regaining legal effect. The pre-2023 bylaw is the subject of a lawsuit filed by developer PureSky Energy in August 2023, in which PureSky alleges that the town’s solar regulations are in violation of state law that prohibits unreasonable regulation of solar energy systems.

Turbines less than 100 feet in height and less than or equal to 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 1.5 times turbine height; turbines between 100 and 150 feet in height and less than or equal to 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 3 times turbine height; and turbines greater than 150 feet in height and/or greater than 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 13 times turbine height. Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (wind) 
In December 2021, the Reno County Commission banned wind development in all zoned areas of the county. The vote to ban wind development in certain areas of the county came three years after residents requested that the commission impose a moratorium on wind development, ostensibly in response to news that NextEra was purchasing leases for a potential wind farm in the county. As of December 2021, a moratorium on commercial wind development was scheduled to run through March 2022. As of February 2023, the county’s zoning regulations provide that, “[i]n order to provide for an incorporated city to extend its corporate boundary and increase its tax base, no turbine shall be located within 1 mile of an incorporated city boundary.” Wind farms are permitted, however, in a designated Commercial Wind Energy Conversion Systems District in the unincorporated part of the county.

As of April 2019, twelve of the fifteen towns within Henry County had passed resolutions establishing buffer zones where no wind projects could be built. These buffers extend approximately 4 miles around each town. The twelve towns included Cadiz, Sulphur Springs, Kennard, Blountsville, Greensboro, Lewisville, Mount Summit, Springport, Straughn, and Middletown. In May 2019, Indiana passed a law limiting municipalities’ authority to enact such buffer zones going forward and voiding any such ordinances or resolution adopted after December 31, 2018. Eleven of the Henry County town resolutions were grandfathered in under the law, but the town of Middletown’s was not.

Rule 2: Capacity Cap (solar)
S.B. 583, codified at W.V. Code §24-2-1o, limits utility-scale solar generation capacity in several ways. The law prohibits any single solar generation facility from having a generating capacity greater than 200 MW, and the law sets a cumulative generating capacity limit of 400 MW for all solar generation facilities “operating at any given time, and for which rate recovery is provided by the commission under this section.” The law also prohibits solar generation facilities from “hav[ing] a generating capacity greater than 50 megawatts until such time as 85 percent of that . . . facility’s annual energy output is being sold or is contracted to be sold to residential, commercial, or industrial customers pursuant to a renewable special contract or renewable tariff.” After that point, the facility’s generating capacity can expand in increments no greater than 50 MW until the facility again reaches the 85% benchmark.

Rule 1: Ban/Moratorium (solar) 
On May 23, 2019, the Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development adopted regulations that restrict the construction of solar facilities on certain categories of farmland. The new rules do not allow solar facilities that use, occupy, or cover more than 12 acres of prime farmland or 20 acres of other farmland unless an exception applies. The regulations effectively prohibit commercial-scale solar projects from 86% of the Willamette Valley.

Rule 6b: Setback Restriction (wind) 
In May 2019, Oklahoma Governor Kevin Sitt signed House Bill 2118 which establishes a setback requirement of 1.5 nautical miles for the construction of individual wind turbines near military airspace, including military training routes, runway approaches, drop zones and bombing ranges. The law requires developers to submit to the Corporation Commission and the Oklahoma Aeronautics Commission a “Determination of No Hazard” from the Federal Aviation Administration and documentation showing that any adverse impacts to the Department of Defense have been resolved. Two weeks after the passage of the bill, NextEra Energy cancelled two proposed wind projects: Minco V and Crowder.

S.B. 52 which took effect October 11, 2021, gives counties the power to veto specific projects and to declare themselves categorically off-limits to large renewable energy projects. Specifically, the law allows counties to adopt binding resolutions to (a) prohibit or limit the construction of a proposed project; and/or (b) designate a “restricted area” in which wind projects of at least 5 MW and solar projects of at least 50 MW are prohibited or otherwise limited. Renewable energy developers must also receive project approval from the Ohio Power Siting Board (OPSB), giving opponents a second opportunity to contest projects if they do not succeed in lobbying the county government for a resolution.

Rule 1: Ban/Moratorium (wind) | Rule 1: Ban/Moratorium (solar) 
On May 3, 2023, the state adopted a law directing the New York Power Authority (NYPA) to develop renewable energy projects “to support the state’s renewable energy goals established pursuant to the climate leadership and community protection act.” While the law generally encourages renewable energy development, it places two significant limitations on where renewable energy facilities may be sited. First, the law specifies that NYPA shall not develop renewable energy generation projects on “land used in agricultural production . . . unless [the] project is in furtherance of an agrivoltaics project” (i.e., unless the project is designed to accommodate dual-use farming and energy production). Second, the law provides that NYPA “shall . . . not build on lands located upon any Native American territory or reservation . . . except through voluntary sale or other agreement for such use with the consent of the relevant nation.”

Rule 1: Ban/Moratorium (wind) 
In July 2021, Governor Janet Mills signed into law L.D. 1619, sponsored by Senator Mark Lawrence. With some exceptions, the law permanently banned the development of all offshore wind projects in Maine state waters but allowed the permitting of offshore wind in federal waters if the Governor’s Energy Office developed a planned research strategy for such projects by March 2023. The law also created the Offshore Wind Research Consortium (ORWC) to study the effects of offshore wind energy on the Gulf of Maine. The law was supported by Maine lobstermen, who expressed concerns about the impact of offshore wind on the state’s fishing industry.

Rule 6a and 6b: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind) 
In April 2025, the Arkansas legislature enacted the Wind Energy Development Act (SB437) which was signed into law on April 22, 2025. The law became effective on August 3, 2025, though its implementing rules (adopted on January 14, 2026) are still pending Legislative Council approval. The law  created Arkansas’ first statewide permitting regime for wind energy facilities of at least 5 megawatts (MW) and exceeding 200 feet in height. The law requires a minimum setback from non-participating property lines of 3.5 times the total height of the wind turbines or 2,500 feet, whichever is greater and a 1-mile setback from a school, hospital, nursing home or church. The law provides that the noise level from wind turbines at non-participating dwellings shall not exceed 35 dBA. Among other things, the law also prohibits wind energy facilities from causing interference to radio, television, or internet reception on adjoining properties; requires developers to file insurance policies, acoustics expert reports, and financial security documentation at least 30 days before commencing construction; and requires developers to publish notice of the project at least once per week, for two consecutive weeks, within 30 days before filing the permit application.
column14: Ark. Code Ann. § 23-18-1401 et seq. (Act 945, 2025), https://arkleg.state.ar.us/Bills/Detail.
